newsitem.title: UK: Funds shy on price but see smooth Hong Kong switch.
newsitem.headline: Funds shy on price but see smooth Hong Kong switch.

text.p: Next week's handover of Hong Kong to Chinese administrators holds few fears for fund managers keen for exposure to the mainland but current high valuations are keeping some players sidelined.
The stock market has soared recently on a variety of factors, including the potential of China and the relative underperformance of other markets in the region.
The Hang Seng Index has risen over 26 percent since early April, closing at a record 15,196.79 on Friday.
"You would have been laughed at a few years ago if you said Hong Kong would be handed to China in 1997 with the Hang Seng at 15,000," said one fund manager.
Analysts said international fund flows had supported the recent rally, and added the outlook for the region was positive.

"We like it. We think it has run up very strongly as a market and it may push on further short term just because there is a lot of liquidity there but we think it may consolidate after that," said Michael Ashbridge, fund manager at Save and Prosper, which is running an overweight Hong Kong position.
"In terms of the handover itself we are fairly relaxed about it."

The major risks associated with the handover are a possible social or political clampdown by mainland China, or excessive moves to cool the property market -- a major spur to the equity market and the economy.
Ashbridge said property accounts for about 40 percent of the Hang Seng and 25 percent of GDP is property development.

"The first risk is that they try to introduce severe measures to calm the property market. The problem is that land and property prices are racing away and there needs to be some sort of control brought in and it needs to be done very sensibly."
Rupert Norman, fund manager at M&G Group, said possibly the greatest political risk lay in clumsiness by the Chinese authorities on the implementation of any changes.
"But the people who are running China are so cosmopolitan and switched on that my worries on the clumsiness side are receding as well."

He said there had been signs that incoming Hong Kong chief executive Tung Chee-hwa may cause some ripples by imposing a ministerial form of government and wresting power away from the civil service, which could have an impact in the shorter term.
"But I cannot possibly see how China could intend to do anything to harm Hong Kong when Hong Kong has so much to offer."
He said the market was expensive historically, driven by Chinese mainland and retail money and historically high weightings by institutions.
It had been winning by default to a certain extent in anticipation of a pickup in the Chinese economy, a low interest rate environment and high liquidity.
"The rest of Asia has also been looking very sick."

He said M&G was neutral on Hong Kong, scaling back on an overweight position that had been in place for many years following the market's significant outperformance of the rest of Asia over the last two years.
"We are still positive and I think that a neutral position is justified."
